 2               known and measurable cost adjustments.
 3           •   Future Test Year. The (“Future Test Year”) runs from December 1, 2026
 4               through November 30, 2027. It includes capital additions that entered
 5               service after July 1, 2024 and those expected to be placed in service through
 6               November 30, 2027, along with Base-Period expenses adjusted for known
 7               and measurable changes, such as increases in labor, compensation, and
 8               benefits.

 9   Q.   Does SPS’s filing meet the requirements of the Future Test Year Rule?

10   A.   Yes. In accordance with the rule, SPS has fully explained and justified its Future

11        Test Year costs, has broken down costs by cost center and elements of cost on a

12        jurisdictional basis, and has explained material changes between the Adjusted Base

13        Period and Future Test Year.

14               SPS has also provided data in fully functional electronic format that is

15        electronically linked to SPS’s cost of service model. These electronic files are

16        stored on a ShareFile site and are available to the parties, Commission, and hearing

17        examiner.

18   Q.   What percentage change is SPS requesting with respect to base rates?

19   A.   SPS’s requested New Mexico retail base revenue reflects an increase of

20        $175,354,544, excluding fuel, purchased power, and riders. This reflects an

21        increase of about 24.45% in base revenues and 16.73% in total revenues for the

22        Future Test Year, as shown on Attachment ZEL-4.


                                              18

                                              Zoë E. Lees

 1                   This increase is necessary to align rates with the cost of serving customers

 2        as SPS transitions its generation fleet and provide a reasonable return on SPS’s

 3        capital investment. SPS’s investments in economical renewable generation also

 4        reduce fuel costs.

 5   Q.   What rate of return is SPS requesting in the case?

 6   A.   SPS requests an overall WACC of 8.21% for the Future Test Year. This return

 7        reflects a 56% equity ratio, an authorized ROE of 10.5%, and a cost of debt of

 8        5.29%.

 9                   If rates are not updated, SPS’s Future Test Year ROE would fall to 5.38%,

10        which is too low to attract the investment needed to maintain reliable service. 9 As

11        SPS witness Todd Wehner explains, the scale of capital spending planned for the

12        next several years would strain SPS’s credit metrics without timely rate relief,

13        making it harder for SPS to finance the infrastructure New Mexico customers

14        depend on.

 1   Q.   What factors are driving SPS to file this rate case at this time?

 2   A.   Several factors are increasing SPS’s overall cost of providing reliable, cost-

 3        effective energy to New Mexico customers:

 4           1) Generation-fleet transition: SPS is managing a major shift in its
 5              generation portfolio. It is retiring aging units, extending the lives of
 6              select plants that remain cost-effective or assist in SPS meeting its
 7              2028 winter reliability requirements, and updating its long-term
 8              planning models to reflect current system conditions. These actions
 9              change SPS’s cost structure and will affect depreciation, O&M, and
10              capital-related expenses during the FTY. Filing this case now allows
11              SPS to align rates with those expected costs and ensure continued
12              reliable service as the fleet transitions;
13           2) Other investments to serve retail load growth:
14               a. Generation investments: During the FTY, SPS will place in
15                  service four solar and battery projects approved in Case No. 23-
16                  00252-UT: Plant X Solar, Cunningham I Solar, Cunningham II
17                  Solar, and Cunningham BESS, as well as the Plant X BESS
18                  proposed in Case No. 25-00066-UT. Additionally, SPS expects
19                  six battery-storage facilities associated with Long-Term
20                  Purchased Power Agreements (“LTPPAs”) to come online. SPS
21                  will seek approval of those LTPPAs later this year and requests
22                  recovery of their capacity costs through base rates in this case
23                  or, alternatively, through SPS’s FPPCAC;
24               b. Transmission and Distribution investments: SPS is investing in
25                  new and upgraded infrastructure to support load growth across
26                  New Mexico. These investments will increase plant-in-service
27                  balances and carrying costs during the FTY. Updating base rates
28                  allows SPS to recover the cost of serving expanding
29                  communities while maintaining safe and reliable service;

 1   actual costs SPS incurs to realize those credits, like transfer costs and financing

 2   costs, no more and no less.

 3          For example, the PTC DTA included in the FTY is based on a forecast of

 4   the Solar Project PTCs through November of 2027. The actual PTCs credited

 5   through fuel will be based on monthly generation. If actual generation falls below

 6   the forecast, customers would otherwise pay a return on the DTA balance based on

 7   higher forecasted credits than those actually received.

 8          Recovering both the costs and benefits of the credits through the FPPCAC

 9   prevents that mismatch. It ensures that customers receive the credits and bear the

10   costs as they occur, eliminating regulatory lag between rate cases and maintaining

11   full symmetry between recovery and crediting.

 1                         X.    RECOVERY OF DEFERRED COSTS

 2   Q.   What topic do you address in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.   In this section of my testimony, I discuss SPS’s request to recover the following

 4        costs that have been deferred in accordance with prior Commission orders: (1) ELI

 5        premiums; (2) investment in legacy meters; and (3) Community Solar regulatory

 6        case and information technology expenses. SPS is proposing to recover these

 7        deferred costs over a two-year amortization period, which SPS will recover before

 8        filing its next rate case.

 9        A.      ELI Premiums (Case No. 25-00030-UT)
10   Q.   Please summarize the Commission’s determination regarding ELI premiums

11        in Case No. 25-00030-UT.

12   A.   In Case No. 25-00030-UT, the Commission approved SPS’s request for an

13        accounting order to defer the incremental cost of ELI premiums to a regulatory

14        asset for future recovery. The Commission found that a nearly 280% increase in

15        premiums between 2023 and 2024 was material, unplanned, and largely outside

16        SPS’s control, driven by volatility in the insurance market and rising wildfire-

17        related risks. The Commission authorized SPS to establish a regulatory asset to

18        track and defer actual ELI premiums above a baseline of $11.6 million, the October

19        2023 renewal amount, through the effective date of rates in this rate case. The

1         Commission emphasized that its order preserved SPS’s right to seek recovery of

 2        those costs in this proceeding but did not prejudge prudence or recovery

 3   Q.   Please describe SPS’s proposal regarding ELI premiums.

 4   A.   Consistent with the Commission’s order in Case No. 25-00030-UT, SPS seeks to

 5        recover the deferred ELI premiums that it has tracked in the approved regulatory

 6        asset. The deferred balance reflects the incremental ELI premiums incurred above

 7        the $11.6 million baseline, net of all applicable tax effects. SPS proposes to recover

 8        the deferred balance through base rates in this proceeding, over a two-year

 9        amortization period and without carrying costs. This approach implements the

10        accounting authority granted in Case No. 25-00030-UT while allowing the

11        Commission to review the prudence and reasonableness of the deferred costs in the

12        context of SPS’s overall revenue requirement.

13   Q.   Why is SPS’s proposal just and reasonable?

14   A.   SPS’s proposal is just and reasonable because it implements the deferral authority

15        the Commission granted in Case No. 25-00030-UT and ensures that SPS can

16        recover prudently incurred, known, and measurable costs. The ELI premiums were

17        necessary to maintain adequate liability coverage for SPS’s operations and, in turn,

18        to protect customers from financial risks, including those associated with wildfire

19        exposure. Recovering the deferred balance through base-rate amortization provides

 1                  IX.    TREATMENT OF FEDERAL TAX CREDITS

 2   Q.   What do you address in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.   In this section, I explain SPS’s proposed treatment of federal tax credits associated

4         with its renewable and storage projects. Specifically, SPS requests authority to:

5         (1)    earn a return on its Deferred Tax Asset (“DTA”) associated with PTCs
6                created by the SPS solar facilities – Plant X Solar, Cunningham I Solar, and
7                Cunningham II Solar (collectively, the “SPS Solar Projects”) – at SPS’s
8                proposed WACC, 8.21%;
 9        (2)    treat the ITCs for the Cunningham BESS and Plant X BESS as follows:
10               (a) amortize the value of the ITCs over five years as a reduction to SPS’s
11               revenue requirement;
12               (b) authorize SPS to accrue a regulatory asset associated with the Plant X
13               BESS transfer costs for future recovery;
14               (c) amortize any transfer costs, capped at 10% of the corresponding ITCs
15               nominal value, over the same amortization period of the ITC value
16               and
17               (d) apply a return at 8.21% to the unamortized balance of the monetized
18               ITC value and transfer costs;
19        (3)    recover reasonable transfer costs for PTCs from the Hale and Sagamore
20               Wind Projects; and
21        (4)    propose an alternative cost recovery method to flow tax-credit benefits and
22               related costs through SPS’s FPPCAC to align benefits and costs in real time.

23               The total company and New Mexico revenue impacts associated with SPS’s

24        proposed treatment of federal tax credits outlined above are discussed by SPS

25        witness Ms. Johnson.

 1        A.       DTA Associated with Solar Project PTCs
 2   Q.   Has the Commission previously addressed treatment of the SPS Solar Project

 3        PTCs and the Cunningham BESS ITC?

 4   A.   Yes. In Case No. 24-00270-UT, the Commission approved a stipulation that

 5        authorized SPS to provide customers with the value of PTCs along with transfer

 6        costs, through the FPPCAC beginning when SPS begins to recover the costs of the

 7        SPS Solar Projects. The stipulation authorized SPS to accrue and earn a return on a

 8        DTA for unused or not yet transferred PTCs but provided that the return would be

 9        established in SPS’s next base rate case.

10                 Regarding the ITC associated with the Cunningham BESS, the Stipulation

11        authorized SPS to: (1) book the ITC as a regulatory liability and seek ratemaking

12        treatment regarding the liability in its next base rate case; and (2) book costs

13        associated with the transfer of the ITC as a regulatory asset and seek ratemaking

14        treatment in its next base rate case.

15   Q.   Please describe SPS’s request regarding ratemaking treatment of the DTA

16        associated with PTCs produced by the SPS Solar Projects.

17   A.   As mentioned above, the DTA will include PTCs that are unused or not yet

18        transferred, SPS proposes to earn a return on the DTA at SPS’s proposed WACC,

19        8.21%.


                                                  78


                                                                                         013
                                     Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                         Zoë E. Lees

 1   Q.   Is SPS’s proposal to earn a return on the DTA just and reasonable?

 2   A.   Yes. SPS is providing customers with the benefit of the PTCs when they are

 3        generated as a reduction to fuel costs, so SPS is essentially financing that reduction

 4        until it can utilize or transfer the PTC and get the cash. SPS’s WACC reflects SPS’s

 5        average cost to finance these costs prior to payment or cost recovery. As a result, it

 6        reasonable for SPS to earn its cost of capital return on the DTA.

 7        B.     Cunningham BESS and Plant X BESS ITCs
 8   Q.   Please describe SPS’s request regarding ratemaking treatment of the

 9        regulatory liability associated with the Cunningham BESS ITC.

10   A.   SPS proposes to amortize the value of the Cunningham BESS ITC over five years

11        as a reduction to the revenue requirement beginning in the FTY (December 2026

12        to November 2027). When the ITC is generated, SPS will monetize its full value,

13        either by using it or transferring it. But customers will receive that value over time

14        through the five-year amortization. Because that unamortized balance of the

15        monetized ITC reduces SPS’s rate base as a regulatory liability, SPS proposes to

16        apply a return on the unamortized amount, at its 8.21% WACC, to remain

17        financially neutral while customers receive the full ITC benefit.

                                           FINAL ORDER

       THIS MATTER comes before the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

(“Commission”) upon Southwestern Public Service Company’s (“SPS”) Application seeking

continuation of its fuel and purchased power cost adjustment clause (“FPPCAC”) and

implementation of other credits, costs and related matters through the FPPCAC (the

“Application”), the Comprehensive Nonunanimous Stipulation (the “Stipulation”) filed by SPS

and other parties, and the Certification of Stipulation (“Certification”) filed by Hearing Examiner

Elizabeth Hurst.

       The Commission approves the Stipulation, as discussed in this order.

                                           BACKGROUND

        1.      On November 21, 2024, 1 SPS filed the Application seeking continued use of its

FPPCAC and requested approval to implement certain other credits, collection of costs, and related

matters through the FPPCAC. The other credits, collection of costs, and related matters referenced

in the Application relate to resources referred to as New SPS Resources. The New SPS Resources

are collectively: (1) the Plant X Solar Project; (2) the Cunningham 1 Solar Project; (3) the

Cunningham 2 Solar Project (together, the (“SPS Solar Projects”); and (4) a battery energy storage

                                          Agreements

      I.    Stipulated Agreements Regarding SPS’s Application

               1.1 Agreement for Continuation of the FPPCAC

       The Signatories agree that SPS’s FPPCAC application is sufficient and complete, and that

it meets the requirements of Rule 17.9.550.17. The Signatories agree to SPS’s continuation of its

monthly fuel factor consistent with and as modified by this Agreement. The Signatories further

agree that the Commission should adopt the additional measures described below to facilitate

treatment through the FPPCAC.

               1.2 Recovery of Certain Matters Through Monthly Factors

       A.      Federal Production Tax Credits Associated with SPS Self-Build Solar Projects.

            1) Signatories agree that, with respect to federal PTCs associated with the SPS Self-

               Build Solar Projects, SPS shall retain 100% of as-generated solar PTCs until New

               Mexico retail cost recovery starts, limited to a maximum of one year following each

               project’s commercial operation date (“COD”). However, SPS shall not retain the

               as-generated solar PTCs if SPS obtains a deferral of the revenue requirement of the

               SPS Self-Build Solar Projects.

            2) Upon the commencement of cost recovery, or deferral of the revenue requirement

               of the SPS Self-Build Solar Projects, SPS shall flow through the value of the as-

               generated solar PTCs to customers through SPS’s monthly FPPCAC factors.

               Ratemaking implementation of this flow-through will be determined in the

                rate case.

B.      Transferability of PTCs.

     1) Signatories agree that SPS may collect through the FPPCAC the transaction costs

        associated with SPS’s sales of PTCs, capped at 10% of the nominal value of the

        PTCs sold, netted against PTCs monthly in the FPPCAC. There will be a prudence

        Projects through base rates, with a rate to be determined in SPS’s next general rate

        case.

 1   Q.   Is SPS’s proposal to earn a return on the DTA just and reasonable?

 2   A.   Yes. SPS is providing customers with the benefit of the PTCs when they are

 3        generated as a reduction to fuel costs, so SPS is essentially financing that reduction

 4        until it can utilize or transfer the PTC and get the cash. SPS’s WACC reflects SPS’s

 5        average cost to finance these costs prior to payment or cost recovery. As a result, it

 6        reasonable for SPS to earn its cost of capital return on the DTA.

 7        B.     Cunningham BESS and Plant X BESS ITCs
 8   Q.   Please describe SPS’s request regarding ratemaking treatment of the

 9        regulatory liability associated with the Cunningham BESS ITC.

10   A.   SPS proposes to amortize the value of the Cunningham BESS ITC over five years

11        as a reduction to the revenue requirement beginning in the FTY (December 2026

12        to November 2027). When the ITC is generated, SPS will monetize its full value,

13        either by using it or transferring it. But customers will receive that value over time

14        through the five-year amortization. Because that unamortized balance of the

15        monetized ITC reduces SPS’s rate base as a regulatory liability, SPS proposes to

16        apply a return on the unamortized amount, at its 8.21% WACC, to remain

17        financially neutral while customers receive the full ITC benefit.

 1   Q.   Please describe SPS’s proposal to apply a return on the deferred balance

 2        associated with the Cunningham BESS ITC.

 3   A.   The deferred balance reflects the timing difference between when SPS receives the

 4        ITC value and when it credits that value to customers over five years. SPS expects

 5        to use or transfer the value of the Cunningham BESS ITC within a year after the

 6        ITC is generated. During the first year, the five-year amortization of the ITC value

 7        creates a deferred asset that increases SPS’s revenue requirement. Once SPS

 8        realizes the ITC’s value, however, the deferred balance becomes a deferred

 9        liability, ultimately reducing the revenue requirement.

10   Q.   Is SPS’s request to earn a return on the deferred balance associated with the

11        Cunningham BESS ITC just and reasonable?

12   A.   Yes. Applying a return reflects SPS’s financing cost for the period that the

13        amortization value is provided to customers before its transfer, and upon transfer,

14        SPS’s cash benefit until the ITC value is fully amortized as a benefit to customers.
